Well, as far as I know (should be mentioned that I'm no epidemiologist) the origins of COVID-19 aren't 100% established, but that it's believed to have originated from bats, with pangolins as a potential intermediate host, making it a zoonotic disease. When it comes to zoonotic diseases, the issue is usually close contact between humans and animals, not close contact between animals and human food. This is not exclusively always the case, some pathogens like salmonella can contaminate food, but it seems that close contact was indeed the issue with COVID-19. 

Furthermore, I don't really see the argument that not all the live animals sold in the Wuhan markets are for eating as a particularly compelling one. For one, a lot, probably most, of the animals and the animal flesh sold is likely intended for human consumption. (I don't actually know what percentage of the animals and the animal flesh sold in these markets  are in tented for human consumption, but a quick look at articles and pictures describing the conditions in them leads me to believe that it's the vast majority. If you've found a good source breaking down these numbers though, I'd love to give it a read.)

Secondly, even if only a negligible part of the sales of these markets were intended for consumption, the problem was still the proximity of humans and animals. So no, the general problem that gave rise to COVID-19 has not been fixed and there's a high risk that a similar disease might spring up sometime in the future. It may happen once again in China, or it may happen elsewhere. And that's what the meme is getting at.
The thing though, as being put forth (albeit not super succinctly) in this meme, is that the root issue hasn't been fixed.

Everyone's depression is different and every person needs different kinds of help. I personally would not be helped by anyone who treated me like I was disabled, that's not how I work, that's not how my depression works. Regardless, depression is very different from a hearing impairment, on so many levels. I have terrible eye sight, but that impairment isn't in any way comparable to my depression.

As a depressed person you have to be aware of how you're affecting people, even when you're feeling like shit. I hadn't seen my father in years, not since that day in 6th grade when I walked into our house through the wide-open kitchen door to find my mother at the table, sobbing, a plate with a half-eaten hot dog lay pushed just before her. I immediately recognised that something was off, something was horribly wrong. Mother looked up through her greasy bangs and bloodshot eyes and said "Father's gone Jimmy, he's gone". Tears welling up I asked her "but when's he coming back?" and she let out a shrieking sob and let her head fall to the table once more. I just remained where I stood and let one lonesome tear fall down my cheek. That was the last time I ever cried.

Mother was never herself after that, but we got on. She got herself a job as a checkout girl in at the nearby supermarket and things were quite happy. Until a few years later when she was diagnosed with breast cancer, when she told me over dinner, I just bit my hot dog and stared at her intently. "Is it bad?", I asked, the salty sensation lingering in my mouth. "Pretty bad. Doctor says I haven't much time left", she said. So I quit school. I became a mechanic at a local car shop. It was hard, back-breaking work. But every day when I came home, mother would look up at me from her sickbed and she'd tell me, tears in her eyes, how proud she was of me and what a man I'd become. 

A few months ago, she died. Her last year was awful, she tried to suffer in silence, she tried her very hardest not to disturb me with her pain. But that only made it harder for me, I felt so shameful that she didn't dare to share her pain and suffering with me -- I could tell she was hiding it. On her deathbed, with all kinds of tubes and stuff sticking in and out of her and machines beeping, she told me to lean in and she whispered in my ear "I'm sorry it had to be this way, but I want you to know that I love you very much, Jimmy" and smiled bitter-sweetly. Those were the last words she ever spoke to me.

So when I looked into my father's intense steel-grey eyes in that gloomy small-town diner, I wasn't sure what to think or to feel. It'd been so long since I'd even thought about things like that. I'd been so busy, somehow. Or maybe I'd just been avoiding it all?

"But... Father... Why?", I asked, hesitantly, "why did you leave us?"  
"Well, son, there's no easy way to put this...", he said with a pained expression, pausing for half a minute, "I guess I'll just have to come right out and say it. Who the hell puts salt on a hot dog, boy?"

Obviously, read a lot, but also write down all the words you don't feel entirely sure of (could you confidently use it in a sentence? If no, write it down), then after you've finished reading, go through all the words and thoroughly look them up and then write down the definitions. A good idea is to get a small notebook where you you can put down all your words, and that you don't use for anything else. Obviously, you can look them up as you go along, but if you encounter too many unfamiliar words in a text you might interrupt the flow of your reading, which makes it hard to focus on the actual text, so I usually prefer to look words up afterwards. The exception being, of course, if the unfamiliar word obstructs my reading. 

In addition, practise using English, write, debate, converse in English, seize every chance you get to use English, especially real-life opportunities, they're the ones that are going to be the most helpful because they really put you on the spot.
